t: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Complete Roadmap

t: Web shell upload via path traversal
x: The upload folder serves PHP as plain text, so a URL-encoded ../ in the filename drops my shell one directory up where it runs.

t: Web shell upload via race condition
x: The upload writes my file into the public folder and validates it afterwards, so a shell fired in that window runs before deletion.

t: Web shell upload via obfuscated file extension
x: A null byte in the filename makes the validator see a harmless .jpg while the filesystem quietly writes out a working .php shell.
The app prints raw database errors, so I CAST a subquery to int and read the admin password straight out of the type error.

t: Web shell upload via extension blacklist bypass
x: Apache reads a .htaccess file straight from the upload folder, so a locked-down extension blacklist still turns into code execution.
The login form leaks valid usernames through response timing, and a spoofed X-Forwarded-For header walks around the IP block.

t: User role can be modified in user profile
x: The email change response leaks a roleId field, so replaying the request with roleid 2 is all it takes to reach the admin panel.
A real username locks after enough bad logins, and that lockout message is what tells me which username actually exists on the site.

t: User ID controlled by request parameter
x: The account page reads the id parameter straight from the request, so swapping wiener for carlos shows me another user's data.

t: URL-based access control can be circumvented
x: A front-end rule blocks external access to /admin, but the backend trusts the X-Original-URL header and I walk right past it.

t: User ID controlled by request parameter with data leakage in redirect
x: Changing my id to carlos bounces me with a 302, but the redirect body still leaks his API key before the browser follows it.

t: Stored XSS into onclick event with angle brackets and double quotes HTML-encoded and single quotes and backslash escaped
x: Quotes and backslashes are escaped inside the stored onclick handler, so I smuggle the quote in as an HTML entity the browser decodes.

t: Stored XSS into anchor href attribute with double quotes HTML-encoded
x: Quotes are encoded but javascript: URLs sail through, so a comment that puts javascript:alert(1) in the link field runs on click.

t: Stored XSS into HTML context with nothing encoded
x: The comment field drops straight into the page with nothing encoded, so a plain script tag fires whenever the post is viewed.
The whitelist only trusts stock.weliketoshop.net, so I smuggle localhost past it with embedded credentials and a double-encoded hash.
Two weak anti-SSRF filters guard the stock check, so I dodge the IP blacklist with 127.1 and the keyword block with double encoding.

t: SSRF with filter bypass via open redirection vulnerability
x: The stock checker only follows local URLs, so I bounce it through the app's own open redirect to reach the admin panel inside.

t: SQL injection with filter bypass via XML encoding
x: The WAF blocks my plain UNION SELECT, so I write the payload as XML hex character references and let the parser decode it.

t: SQL injection attack, listing the database contents on Oracle
x: Oracle has no magic table name, so I read all_tables and all_tab_columns to find the users table and dump its contents.

t: SQL injection attack, querying the database type and version on Oracle
x: Oracle insists every SELECT has a FROM, so the UNION leans on dual and the version banner comes out of the v$version view.

t: Source code disclosure via backup files
x: A hidden /backup directory hands out the application's source, and the database password is sitting there hard-coded in plain sight.
Editing a product description with ${foobar} reveals the FreeMarker engine, whose new() built-in can build an Execute object that runs commands.

t: Server-side template injection with information disclosure via user-supplied objects

t: Server-side template injection in an unknown language with a documented exploit

t: Remote code execution via polyglot web shell upload
x: Magic bytes are the check here, so a file that starts with GIF89a and then carries PHP is both a valid image and a working web shell.

t: Reflected XSS into a JavaScript string with angle brackets and double quotes HTML-encoded and single quotes escaped
x: Angle brackets and double quotes are encoded and single quotes are escaped, so you hand the escaped quote your own backslash.

t: Reflected XSS into a JavaScript string with angle brackets HTML encoded
x: This lab contains a reflected cross-site scripting vulnerability in the search query tracking functionality where angle brackets are encoded. The reflection occurs inside a JavaScript string. To solve

t: Reflected XSS in canonical link tag
x: A reflected XSS lab where your input lands in a canonical link tag with angle brackets escaped, so the payload has to break out of the attribute.
The reset link is built from the X-Forwarded-Host header, so I point it at my exploit server and steal Carlos's reset token.
This lab controls access to certain admin functionality based on the Referer header. You can familiarize yourself with the admin panel by logging in using the credentials `administrator:admin`.
The change-password form trusts a hidden username field, and its mismatch error leaks whether the current password was correct.

t: Multi-step process with no access control on one step
x: This lab has an admin panel with a flawed multi-step process for changing a user's role. You can familiarize yourself with the admin panel by logging in using the credentials `administrator:admin`.
Stored XSS steals Carlos's stay-logged-in cookie, and the MD5 hash inside it cracks offline to his password.

t: Method-based access control can be circumvented
x: This lab implements access controls based partly on the HTTP method of requests. You can familiarize yourself with the admin panel by logging in using the credentials `administrator:admin`.

t: JWT authentication bypass via unverified signature
x: The server never checks the JWT signature at all, so I edit the sub claim to administrator and keep the original signature.

t: JWT authentication bypass via weak signing key
x: The HS256 secret is a plain dictionary word, so I crack it offline with hashcat and re-sign my own token as administrator.

t: JWT authentication bypass via kid header path traversal
x: The kid header is pasted into a key file path, so I traverse to /dev/null and sign the token with an empty key.

t: JWT authentication bypass via jku header injection
x: The jku header names the key-set URL, so I host my own JWKS on the exploit server and point the token at it.

t: JWT authentication bypass via jwk header injection
x: The server trusts the key embedded in the token's jwk header, so I inject my own RSA key and sign as administrator.

t: JWT authentication bypass via flawed signature verification
x: The server accepts the none algorithm, so I strip the signature entirely and sign in as administrator with an unsigned token.

t: JWT authentication bypass via algorithm confusion with no exposed key
x: No public key is published, so I recover the RSA modulus from two JWTs, then sign HS256 with the derived public key.

t: JWT authentication bypass via algorithm confusion
x: The server exposes its RS256 public key and also trusts HS256, so I sign a token with the public key as the HMAC secret.

t: Information disclosure in version control history
x: This lab discloses sensitive information via its version control history. To solve the lab, obtain the password for the administrator user then log in and delete the user carlos.
This lab contains an information disclosure vulnerability on the debug page. To solve the lab, obtain and submit the SECRET_KEY that is exposed on the debug page.
This lab's verbose error messages reveal that it is using a vulnerable version of a third-party framework. To solve the lab, obtain and submit the version number of this framework.

t: File path traversal, validation of start of path
x: The parameter must start with `/var/www/images/`. Satisfy the prefix, then climb straight back out of it with `../`.

t: File path traversal, traversal sequences stripped with superfluous URL-decode
x: The app strips `../`, then decodes again anyway. Double-encoding pushes the traversal past the filter to that second decode.

t: File path traversal, validation of file extension with null byte bypass
x: The app wants a `.png` ending. A null byte ends the string for the filesystem, so `/etc/passwd%00.png` passes both checks.

t: File path traversal, traversal sequences stripped non-recursively
x: The filter deletes `../` in one pass and stops. `....//` reassembles into a working traversal after that pass.

t: File path traversal, traversal sequences blocked with absolute path bypass
x: Traversal sequences are blocked this time, but absolute paths are not. `filename=/etc/passwd` skips the base directory entirely.

t: Exploiting NoSQL operator injection to bypass authentication
x: The JSON login lets you swap a string value for a MongoDB operator object, so the query matches the admin without a password.

t: Exploiting NoSQL operator injection to extract unknown fields
x: With $where in the JSON login you can run JavaScript against carlos's user document and pull his reset token one character at a time.

t: Exploiting NoSQL injection to extract data
x: The user lookup is a $where predicate, so this.password[0] and this.password.length let me brute-force the admin password one character at a time.

t: DOM XSS in jQuery selector sink using a hashchange event
x: jQuery parses a hashchange value as HTML when it is used as a selector, so the hash has to look like a tag and print() runs.

t: DOM XSS in innerHTML sink using source location.search
x: location.search flows into innerHTML, which never runs script tags, so an image with a broken src and an onerror handler does the work.

t: DOM XSS in jQuery anchor href attribute sink using location.search source
x: jQuery writes location.search into the back link's href, so a javascript: URL there fires on click. No server reflection needed at all.

t: DOM XSS in document.write sink using source location.search
x: The search term goes straight into the page through document.write, so a crafted query string is all it takes to run my JavaScript.
MongoDB runs my category through a JavaScript $where predicate, so a quote throws a JS error and '||1||' returns every document, unreleased products included.

t: DOM XSS in document.write sink using source location.search inside a select element
x: Same document.write sink, except the reflection lands inside a select element, so you break out of the option list first.
The login rate limiter counts HTTP requests, not login attempts. Aliases packed every candidate password into one mutation.

t: Broken brute-force protection, multiple credentials per request
x: The login takes JSON, so I drop every candidate password into one array and a single request guesses the whole wordlist.
The stay-logged-in cookie is base64 of username plus an MD5 of the password, so a wordlist and Burp payload processing crack Carlos.
Three failed logins block my IP, but a successful login resets the counter, so I alternate my own account with Carlos's guesses.

t: Blind SQL injection with time delays
x: One request, one clock: PostgreSQL pg_sleep(10) spliced into the tracking cookie with || and a comment, and the ten-second wait is the entire signal.

t: Blind SQL injection with time delays and information retrieval
x: PostgreSQL pg_sleep(10) hidden behind a CASE and stacked onto the cookie with a semicolon. A ten-second reply is the yes, and SUBSTRING walks the password out.

t: Blind SQL injection with out-of-band data exfiltration
x: Oracle's XMLTYPE external entity resolves a URL I build at query time, so the admin password rides out of the database inside a Collaborator DNS lookup.

t: Blind SQL injection with out-of-band interaction
x: The query runs async and never touches the response, so I force Oracle to look up a Collaborator hostname and take the DNS hit as proof the injection fired.

t: Blind SQL injection with conditional responses
x: A Welcome back line is the only bit each request gives me. I flip it with an AND condition and pull the admin password out one character at a time.

t: Blind OS command injection with time delays
x: The feedback form runs my input through a shell, and the response never shows it. A ten-second ping is the only proof I get.

t: Blind SQL injection with conditional errors
x: The response never changes, only its status code: an Oracle CASE wrapping TO_CHAR(1/0) throws a 500 when my guess is right and a 200 when it is not.

t: Blind OS command injection with output redirection
x: The command output is lost, but the web server serves a writable directory. Redirect the output into a file there and fetch it.

t: Blind OS command injection with out-of-band data exfiltration
x: Collaborator proves the shell runs. This time the command output itself rides out inside the DNS name.

t: Blind OS command injection with out-of-band interaction
x: No output and no writable web path. So I make the server resolve a Burp Collaborator name and watch the lookup arrive.
